passages.t: Malta, a fire, and a viper
passages.happening:
Once they are safely ashore, they learn that the island is called Malta (verse 1). “The islanders showed us extraordinary kindness” (verse 2). It is raining and cold, so they light a fire and welcome everyone (verse 2).

Paul gathers a bundle of sticks. As he puts them on the fire, a viper, driven out by the heat, fastens itself on his hand (verse 3). The islanders see the snake hanging from his hand and say, “Surely this man is a murderer. Although he was saved from the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live” (verse 4). But Paul shakes the creature off into the fire and suffers no harm (verse 5). The islanders wait for him to swell up or suddenly fall dead. When nothing happens after a long time, they change their minds and say he is a god (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Malta lies south of Sicily. Where exactly the ship struck is not known for sure. Tradition places it at St Paul's Bay, on the island's north-east coast, and the map on the book page marks it there.

The Berean Standard Bible calls the people ‘the islanders’. Luke's Greek word is barbaroi. In English that sounds like ‘barbarians’, but in Greek it meant simply people whose language was not Greek. It was not an insult here. Luke praises these people warmly: their kindness was ‘extraordinary’. Two hundred and seventy-six soaked, half-starved strangers came out of the sea, and the islanders built them a fire in the rain.

Their reaction to the snake shows what they believed. ‘Justice’ here is a name. Greeks pictured Justice as a goddess, Dike, who paid back the guilty. The islanders reason that this man must be a murderer: he escaped the sea, but Justice has caught up with him anyway. Then, when he does not die, they swing to the opposite idea: he must be a god. The crowd at Lystra did the same (14:11). Luke records both judgments without comment. Paul is neither a murderer nor a god. He is a servant of the God who had promised he would stand before Caesar (27:24).
passages.ot:
God's protection of his servants in danger is a Psalm's promise: “You will tread on the lion and cobra; you will trample the young lion and serpent” (Psalm 91:13). Jesus told his followers he had given them authority over the power of the enemy (Luke 10:19).

But the same Psalm was quoted by the devil to tempt Jesus to throw himself from the temple, and Jesus answered from Deuteronomy, “Do not put the Lord your God to the test” (Matthew 4:7; Deuteronomy 6:16).

The welcome of strangers by people outside Israel echoes Abraham, who ran to welcome three travellers and brought water and bread (Genesis 18:2-5).
passages.hard:
Is this a pattern for Christians, or a test of faith? No. Luke tells what happened to Paul on one cold day on Malta. Paul did not pick up the snake to prove anything. He was gathering firewood, it bit him, and God kept him from harm, as he had kept him from the sea. God had said Paul must stand before Caesar (27:24). Nothing in this passage tells anyone to handle snakes, or to treat surviving danger as proof of faith.

Some people read this story beside Mark 16:18, “they will pick up snakes with their hands”. That verse belongs to the longer ending of Mark, which the earliest manuscripts do not have. The note on Mark 16:15-20 explains this, and says plainly that no church should build a practice on a verse from that disputed ending alone. Since the early 1900s, a few churches have handled venomous snakes in worship, and people have died.

So say it plainly: Christians must not handle snakes, or put themselves in danger to test God, on the strength of these verses. And they must not refuse medical care because of them. Jesus himself refused to test God: “Do not put the Lord your God to the test” (Matthew 4:7). Paul was protected in the course of his work, not in a show. Seeking a doctor is not a lack of faith. Luke, the companion who wrote this chapter, is called a physician in Paul's letters (Colossians 4:14).
passages.asks: People with no knowledge of Israel's God showed ‘extraordinary kindness’ to shipwrecked strangers. Ask whether you have ever been surprised by the goodness of people outside your faith, and whether you have thanked them. And the islanders judged Paul twice, first a murderer and then a god, and were wrong both times. Ask how quickly you judge people by what happens to them.

passages.t: Publius's father, and the sick of the island
passages.happening:
Nearby is an estate belonging to Publius, the chief official of the island. He welcomes them and looks after them kindly for three days (verse 7). His father is in bed, sick with fever and dysentery. Paul goes in to see him, prays, lays his hands on him, and heals him (verse 8).

After this, the rest of the sick on the island come and are cured too (verse 9). The islanders honour them in many ways, and when they are ready to sail they give them what they need (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Luke calls Publius ‘the chief official of the island’; in Greek, ‘the first man’. Inscriptions from the Maltese islands are reported to use a similar title for a leading official, a small detail that fits the place.

‘Fever and dysentery’ means a high temperature and a serious illness of the bowels, which could kill. Paul prays first, then lays his hands on the man. The healing is God's answer to prayer, not a power of Paul's own.

The writer, the ‘we’ of the story, was there. Paul's letters name ‘Luke, the beloved physician’ (Colossians 4:14), and many think he is the writer. The text says only that the islanders ‘honored us in many ways’ (verse 10). It does not say that Luke treated anyone, and these notes will not add it.

The chapter began with the islanders caring for the shipwrecked. Now the shipwrecked bring healing to the islanders. Kindness flows both ways. And when the travellers leave three months later, the islanders give them what they need for the voyage.

A word for anyone who has prayed for someone who was not healed: this passage does not mean your prayer was too weak. The note on Acts 3:1-10 speaks to that sorrow, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.ot:
Healing through prayer runs through the Old Testament. Elijah prayed over the widow's son and “the LORD listened to the voice of Elijah, and the child's life returned to him” (1 Kings 17:22). Elisha's prayer brought back the Shunammite's son (2 Kings 4:33-35). Naaman, a foreigner, was healed by Israel's God (2 Kings 5:14).

And the welcome given to God's servants is rewarded, as with the widow of Zarephath, who shared her last bread with Elijah (1 Kings 17:15-16).
passages.asks: Publius welcomed strangers, and his own father was healed. Ask whether you are open to receiving good from people you have helped, and to giving help to people who helped you. And Paul prayed before he laid his hands on the sick. Ask whether prayer is the first thing you bring to the sickness around you.

passages.t: To Rome by the Appian Way
passages.happening:
After three months they sail in an Alexandrian ship that has wintered at the island, with the Twin Brothers as its figurehead (verse 11). They put in at Syracuse for three days (verse 12), then sail to Rhegium. A south wind comes up, and on the second day they reach Puteoli (verse 13). There they find brothers in the faith, who invite them to stay a week. “And so we came to Rome” (verse 14).

The believers in Rome have heard about them and come out as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns to meet them. When Paul sees them, he is encouraged and thanks God (verse 15). In Rome, Paul is allowed to live on his own, with a soldier to guard him (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Three months on Malta brings them to the end of winter. Then another Alexandrian ship, probably another grain ship, carries them on. Its figurehead was the Twin Brothers, Castor and Pollux, the gods sailors prayed to in a storm. Luke notes it without comment. Paul sails to Rome under the sign of gods he did not worship, kept safe by the God he did.

Syracuse was a great city of Sicily. Rhegium lay at the toe of Italy. Puteoli was the great harbour on the Bay of Naples where grain ships from Alexandria unloaded for Rome. And there, far from any church Paul had founded, he finds believers waiting. The faith had reached Italy before Paul did.

From Puteoli the road ran north to Rome. The Appian Way was one of the great roads of Italy, and the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns were two stopping places south of the city. In a world where travel was slow and costly, walking out to meet someone was a public act of honour. The believers of Rome gave it to a man in chains. Paul had written to them years before, longing to see them (Romans 1:11). Now he sees them, and he takes courage.

In Rome Paul is held under a lighter kind of guard, in lodgings of his own, with a soldier always with him. He is a prisoner, but he can receive visitors.
passages.ot: The welcome of the brothers on the road recalls the welcome of God's people for one another in the Psalms: “how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in harmony” (Psalm 133:1). And the gospel arriving in the city of the nations fulfils Isaiah's vision of God's word going out from Jerusalem to all peoples: “For the law will go forth from Zion, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem” (Isaiah 2:3).
passages.asks: Believers Paul had never met walked for miles to meet a prisoner, and he took courage when he saw them. Ask whom you could encourage simply by going out to meet them. And ask whether you thank God, as Paul did, for the people who come out to meet you on hard roads.

passages.t: Paul meets the Jewish leaders of Rome
passages.happening:
Three days later Paul calls together the leaders of the Jews in Rome. He tells them, “Brothers, although I have done nothing against our people or the customs of our fathers, I was taken prisoner in Jerusalem and handed over to the Romans” (verse 17). The Romans wanted to release him, finding nothing deserving death (verse 18). But when the Jews objected, he had to appeal to Caesar, “even though I have no charge to bring against my nation” (verse 19). “It is because of the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain” (verse 20).

The leaders reply that they have received no letters about him from Judea, and none of the brothers from there has reported anything bad about him (verse 21). But they want to hear his views, “because we know that people everywhere are speaking against this sect” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Paul's first act in Rome is to meet the leaders of the Jewish community. It is his lifelong pattern: to the Jew first. He calls them ‘Brothers’. He has done nothing against ‘our people’. He brings no charge against ‘my nation’. He is in chains ‘because of the hope of Israel’. Everything in his words says that he is one of them, and that his faith in Jesus is Israel's own hope.

‘When the Jews objected’ (verse 19) means the leaders in Jerusalem who opposed his release. It is not a word about the Jewish people, and Paul is speaking to Jews who have done him no wrong; the note on Acts 13:42-47 sets out how this site reads such phrases.

The Roman leaders' answer is generous and fair. They have heard nothing bad about Paul. No letters have come from Judea. Readers suggest reasons: winter travel, or a decision in Jerusalem not to follow the case to Rome. Luke does not say. They know the followers of Jesus are spoken against everywhere, but they do not condemn Paul. They want to hear him for themselves.

There had been a Jewish community in Rome for a long time. Some years earlier, the emperor Claudius had ordered Jews to leave the city, as Acts mentions (18:2), and the book page explains what is known of it. By now Jews had returned, and Paul's own letter to Rome shows Jewish and Gentile believers in the church there.
passages.ot:
The hope of Israel is the hope of the Prophets: God would gather his people, send his Messiah, and raise the dead. “I will appoint over them one shepherd, My servant David” (Ezekiel 34:23), and “many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake” (Daniel 12:2).

The fair hearing the Roman leaders offer is what the Law asked of every judge: “hear both small and great alike” (Deuteronomy 1:17).
passages.asks: The Jewish leaders of Rome refused to condemn Paul on rumour and asked to hear him themselves. Ask whether you give people that fairness, especially people whose views you have only heard spoken against. And Paul called them ‘Brothers’ and said he had no charge against his nation. Ask how you speak about people who disagree with your faith.

passages.t: Some convinced, some not, and Isaiah's words
passages.happening:
They set a day, and many come to Paul's lodging. From morning to evening he explains and testifies about the kingdom of God, persuading them about Jesus “from the Law of Moses and the Prophets” (verse 23). “Some of them were convinced by what he said, but others refused to believe” (verse 24).

They disagree among themselves and begin to leave after Paul's final word (verse 25). He quotes Isaiah: “Go to this people and say, ‘You will be ever hearing but never understanding; you will be ever seeing but never perceiving’” (verse 26), for their heart has grown dull, and they have closed their eyes (verse 27). “Be advised, therefore, that God's salvation has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will listen!” (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
A long day of teaching from the Scriptures, and a divided result. ‘Some of them were convinced by what he said, but others refused to believe.’ It is what has happened in town after town in Acts. Some Jews believe, some do not. The leaders of Rome are not a single block: they argue among themselves as they leave.

Your Bible may have no verse 29. Some later manuscripts add that the Jews left, arguing among themselves. The earliest manuscripts do not have it, and many think it was added to smooth the step from verse 28 to verse 30, so most modern Bibles leave it out or put it in a footnote.

Then Paul quotes Isaiah 6. These were the words God gave Isaiah when he sent him to his own people: they would hear and not understand. Jesus used the same words of those who heard his parables (Luke 8:10). In Isaiah they are a prophet's grief over his own nation, spoken from inside Israel, not a verdict from outside it.

Read verse 28 with the whole of Acts. Paul has said this kind of thing twice before. In Pisidian Antioch: ‘We now turn to the Gentiles’ (13:46). In Corinth: ‘From now on I will go to the Gentiles’ (18:6). Each time it was a turn in one place, and each time he went to the synagogue first in the next town. Here there is no next town in the story. But Paul goes on ‘welcoming all who came to visit him’ (verse 30), and that would include Jews.
passages.ot:
Paul quotes the call of Isaiah. In the Berean Standard Bible's Isaiah the words read, “Be ever hearing, but never understanding; be ever seeing, but never perceiving” (Isaiah 6:9), and, “Otherwise they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts, and turn and be healed” (Isaiah 6:10). Acts gives them in the slightly different words of the Greek translation.

Isaiah asked how long this would last, and God's answer ended with a seed of hope: the felled tree would leave a stump, and “the holy seed will be a stump in the land” (Isaiah 6:13). Isaiah also foresaw salvation reaching the nations: “I will also make You a light for the nations” (Isaiah 49:6).
passages.hard:
Does the end of Acts mean that God has given up on the Jewish people? No. Verse 28 is not God's last word on Israel.

Paul's closing words have sometimes been read as a final rejection of Israel, and that reading fed Christian contempt for Jews in later centuries. That reading is false, and Christians must reject it plainly. This site rejects it. The text itself is more careful. Paul calls the Roman Jews ‘Brothers’, says he has no charge against his nation, and wears his chain ‘because of the hope of Israel’ (verse 20). Some of his hearers are persuaded (verse 24), as Jews have been all through Acts, and the first believers were all Jews.

Paul had already written to the believers in this very city, a few years earlier, before he took the gift to Jerusalem (Romans 15:25). In that letter he gives three chapters to this question (Romans 9 to 11). He writes, “I ask then, did God reject His people? Certainly not! I am an Israelite myself” (Romans 11:1). He writes that salvation has come to the Gentiles “to make Israel jealous” (Romans 11:11), not to replace them. He says, “And so all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:26), and, “For God's gifts and His call are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29).

Christians read Romans 11:26 in more than one way. Many think it promises a great turning of the Jewish people to Christ before the end. Others take ‘all Israel’ to mean the whole people of God, Jews and Gentiles together. Others take it to mean the full number of Jewish believers through all of history. These notes do not choose between them, or say how the promise will be fulfilled. On any reading, Paul's own words stand: “God did not reject His people, whom He foreknew” (Romans 11:2).

Readers also differ on what Luke meant by ending here. Some read the scene as Luke's verdict that the mission to Israel as a whole has run its course and the future lies with the Gentiles. Others read it as a sad but open door. Acts does not give a verdict on the Jewish people.

Over the centuries this ending, like the ‘you crucified’ verses, has been used against Jewish people. The note on Acts 2:22-28 explains how verses like these were turned against the Jewish people, and why this site rejects that reading. Acts leaves Paul, at the very end, still calling his own people ‘Brothers’.
passages.asks: Paul taught from morning to evening, and some believed and some did not. Ask whether you can keep speaking the truth faithfully without controlling how people respond. And Paul quoted Isaiah's grief, not a curse. Ask whether you speak of people who reject your faith with grief and love, as Paul did of his own people, or with contempt.

passages.t: Two years, and the word unhindered
passages.happening:
“Paul stayed there two full years in his own rented house, welcoming all who came to visit him” (verse 30). “Boldly and freely he proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ” (verse 31).

And there the book ends.
passages.hearers:
Two years in a rented house, a soldier always beside him, and the door open to ‘all who came’. Paul is still a prisoner. He is still waiting for his case to be heard. Yet the last words of Acts are about freedom. ‘Boldly and freely’: the Greek ends with one word, ‘unhindered’. The man is in chains; the word is not.

Most date these two years to about AD 60 to 62. Many scholars think Paul wrote some of his letters from prison here, Philippians, Colossians, Philemon and Ephesians, though others place them at Caesarea or Ephesus. In Philippians he wrote that his imprisonment had “actually served to advance the gospel” (Philippians 1:12), and that the whole palace guard knew he was in chains for Christ.
passages.ot: The last scene fulfils the promise of the first chapter, which drew on Isaiah: the Servant would be “a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6). Jesus had said his witnesses would go “to the ends of the earth” (Acts 1:8). And the word that cannot be chained is the word Isaiah praised: “The grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of our God stands forever” (Isaiah 40:8).
passages.hard:
Why does Acts stop here, without telling how Paul's trial ended or how he died? Readers give different answers, and the book page sets them out. Some think Luke wrote at this very time, before the trial was decided, and simply brought the story up to his own day. Others think the outcome was known to his readers and was not the point: the story was heading for Rome all along, and its last words show the message preached there without hindrance, so the goal was reached. Some have suggested Luke planned a third book. These notes do not choose between these views.

What happened to Paul? Acts does not say, and what we have comes from later Christian writers, as tradition. The letter called 1 Clement, written from Rome and usually dated near the end of the first century, speaks of Paul as having died as a witness, after preaching in the east and the west and reaching, it says, the limits of the west. What that phrase means is argued: Rome, or Spain, where Paul had hoped to go (Romans 15:24). Eusebius, a church historian writing in the early fourth century, says that Paul was released after his first defence, preached again, and was later brought back to Rome and put to death under Nero. Christian tradition holds that both Peter and Paul died in Rome under Nero. Scholars are divided on whether Paul was released in between.

In 2 Timothy, Paul writes from prison, facing death, “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith” (2 Timothy 4:7). Whether that letter comes from these two years, from a later imprisonment, or, as some scholars think, from a follower writing in his name, is part of the same argument.

So where does the story go from here? Acts stops, but its story does not. The letters Paul wrote from prison carry his voice on: to the church at Philippi, to the believers at Colossae, to a slave owner named Philemon, and, if they are his, to the churches of Asia. The rest of the New Testament takes up the church's life in the years Acts does not tell.

And the story goes on past the New Testament. The word that went from Jerusalem to Rome went on from Rome, carried by people whose names no one wrote down, until it reached the reader of these notes. Luke leaves the last door of his book open, with Paul ‘welcoming all who came’. Many readers find in that open door an invitation: the story is not finished.
passages.asks: Paul, in chains, spent two years welcoming everyone who came to his door. Ask what you are doing with the time and the place you have, even if it is not the place you would have chosen. And Acts ends with an open door. Ask where your own part in its continuing story is, and who might be waiting at your door.
